_doc: Street centreline paths and the visible travelled strips for the 1 July 1835 scene. The platted corridors are 80 ft (24.384 m) wide; the bare or thinly grassed track drawn inside one is narrower and explicitly conjectural. Paths are analytic extensions of the committed street-control module and the 1834 plats, not traces of modern pavement. A path is clipped wherever the heightfield is water, so a platted line never paints an invented ford across a branch of the river. Surface classes follow chicago_dpw_1891_streets: earth only on this date. South Water and Lake are the early principal graded/turnpiked routes; the fall-1836 work on Canal, western Lake, and Randolph is not backdated. The Gurdon Hubbard La Salle segment is omitted as a special improvement because his petition is dated twelve days after this scene.
surface_standard: No gravel or hard paving is shown. 'graded' and 'turnpiked' are rendered as drained or thrown-up earth with wagon wear; ordinary streets are worn native soil with a grassy crown and margins.

streets.note: The curved west approach follows the dry south bank resolved by the committed heightfield; east of Franklin the line follows the modern Wacker control used by the structure placements but is shifted into the dry half of the platted riverfront corridor. The street stops at the United States Reservation, matching the 1833 order. Track width and ruts are visual interpretation, not measurements.

The two verified Lake intersections fix the line. The official chronology calls Lake one of the two principal early turnpiked and graded streets, but separately dates its western extension to Desplaines to fall 1836; the 1835 visual treatment therefore stays earth and does not imply that every western block had already received the later work.
The fall-1836 turnpiking recorded for Randolph is deliberately not backdated.

Hubbard's petition says he had graded and thrown up the short South Water-to-Lake segment, but is dated 13 July 1835. On the scene date twelve days earlier this path therefore receives no special improved treatment.

The line uses the road-only Kinzie control already adopted by the North Branch bridge rather than the queued five-node bikeway-inclusive GCP. Its recorded turnpiking belongs to fall 1836 and is not backdated.

A schematic bank-following path used for orientation and readout. The 1834 sheets and surviving name establish the corridor, but the committed street module does not yet carry enough control to claim this curve as a trace.

THE ROAD THE FORT PLAINLY HAD, DRAWN AT THE RECONSTRUCTED TIER, and which part is which is stated rather than implied. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED: the fort had large gates north and south - Juliette Kinzie inside it in 1831, Andreas independently, and a break in each of those two walls and in neither of the others on the 1830 Harrison plan - and the garrison garden's own record reads off that same plan that the plot lies 'west of the road'. So the plan draws a road on the reservation, and a road that is east of that garden and arrives at that gate has to run about here. WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED: nobody traced this line, nobody measured it, and no source names it. The 1835 name is DESCRIPTIVE, not a proper name; the 2026 name is the street that runs over this ground today, not a descent of name. THE WESTERN REACH IS THE INVENTION AND IT IS THE REASON THIS RECORD IS RECONSTRUCTED: South Water Street stops at the United States Reservation, matching the 1833 order, so the connection from the town to the fort gate was never a platted street - it is drawn because a garrisoned post that mustered, traded and drew its stores through the town had a way in, and a visitor who walks east out of South Water Street should find one instead of trackless prairie. The line is routed clear of the garden's east corner and of the Beaubien buildings, and it is clipped by the water mask like every other track, so it makes honest gaps rather than fords where the ground is wet.
